transcript.content: Hello. I'm glad you're here today. What brings you in to see me?

I'm here because I'm feeling really overwhelmed by how awful my skin looks. I have these terrible acne scars and blemishes all over my face, and it's making me feel completely miserable. I just can't stop focusing on how bad it is.
Have family, friends, or doctors noticed these blemishes as well, or do they tell you that they can't see them or that your skin looks fine?

Everyone I ask—my family, friends, and even other doctors—keeps telling me my skin looks completely fine and that they can't see anything. It is incredibly frustrating because the scars are so obvious to me, and I feel like they're just saying that to be nice or aren't looking closely enough. I don't understand how they can miss them.
Do you find yourself spending a significant amount of time checking your skin in the mirror, picking at it, or trying to cover it up?

Yes, I spend hours staring in the mirror, obsessively picking at any tiny bumps to try and 'fix' them, which just makes it worse. Then I feel forced to use heavy layers of makeup to cover it all up before I can even think about letting anyone see me.

It sounds incredibly exhausting to carry this level of distress every day. Do you ever feel there is a possibility that your mind might be making these blemishes seem much more severe to you than they actually are?

I've tried to consider that, but it's just so hard to believe my mind is exaggerating it. When I look in the mirror, the scars look absolutely devastating and completely obvious to me. They feel so incredibly real and severe that I just can't see it any other way.
How has this distress and the time spent on your skin impacted your daily life, such as your ability to work, go to school, or spend time with friends?
I'm not really sure, and I haven't thought much about how it affects my work or social life. I just know that the preoccupation itself takes up almost all of my time and energy every single day.

latest_inference.note: The patient meets all DSM-5 criteria for Body Dysmorphic Disorder, including preoccupation with non-existent or slight physical flaws (skin blemishes/scars), repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, skin picking, and camouflaging with makeup), and significant distress/impairment in daily functioning. Their insight is poor/absent, which is consistent with the 'absent insight/delusional beliefs' specifier of BDD rather than a separate delusional disorder. No further questioning is required to confirm this diagnosis.
